chapterMetaData.title: Monitoring Resources
chapterMetaData.sourceBook: Chap 11 - MCA Microsoft Certified Associate Azure Administrator Study Guide Exam AZ-104 - Donald Robb.pdf

knowledgeKeyPoints.title: Azure Monitor Telemetry: Metrics vs. Logs
knowledgeKeyPoints.summary: Azure Monitor collects telemetry data to analyze system performance, health, and availability [183]. Telemetry is separated into two primary data stores: Metrics and Logs [184]. Metrics are lightweight, numerical values representing system state at a specific time, allowing for real-time monitoring and alerting [183, 184]. Logs contain structured or unstructured records (such as performance counters and syslog) stored in Log Analytics and queried using the rich Kusto Query Language (KQL) [184, 192].

knowledgeKeyPoints.title: Azure Activity Log Auditing
knowledgeKeyPoints.summary: The Azure Activity Log provides subscription-level auditing to track administrative operations, including service configuration changes, recommendations, Service Health events, and Azure Policy compliance [185]. It logs who committed the operation, what was done, and when it occurred [185]. All write operations (PUT, POST, DELETE) are logged, while read operations (GET) are never recorded [185]. Activity logs can be filtered by resource type, category, or initiator [186].

knowledgeKeyPoints.title: Azure Alerts and Action Groups
knowledgeKeyPoints.summary: Azure Alerts notify administrators or automate remediations when resource telemetry crosses defined thresholds [183, 192]. Alert rules consist of a target scope (such as virtual machines), a criteria condition (like CPU Percentage metrics), and an action group [187, 188]. Action Groups define the notification preferences (such as emailing specific Azure Resource Manager roles or sending SMS/push notifications) and automation targets (including Logic Apps, Azure Functions, Runbooks, Webhooks, or Event Hubs) [188, 192].

knowledgeKeyPoints.title: Network Watcher Diagnostic and Troubleshooting Tools
knowledgeKeyPoints.summary: Network Watcher includes diagnostic utilities for diagnosing VM connectivity issues [193]. IP Flow Verify checks if a security rule blocks traffic based on 5-tuple parameters, indicating which Network Security Group (NSG) rule blocks communication [189, 193]. Next Hop identifies the next hop type and associated route table to verify User-Defined Routes (UDR) or system routing [189, 193]. Connection Troubleshoot diagnoses end-to-end connectivity from a VM to another VM, IP address, URI, or FQDN, generating latency and hop-by-hop analysis [190, 193].

knowledgeKeyPoints.title: Network Watcher Advanced Monitoring & Visualizations
knowledgeKeyPoints.summary: Network Watcher offers advanced monitoring capabilities including Packet Capture, NSG Flow Logs, and Topology mapping [193]. Packet Capture performs on-demand captures of VM packet traffic based on parameters like time limits or byte counts [190]. NSG Flow Logs record IP flow traffic (source/destination IP, ports, protocol, and allow/deny action) and store them in an Azure storage account or Log Analytics workspace [191, 193]. Topology generates a graphical visualization of deployed virtual network resources and their relationships [191, 193].

highYieldNotes.whyItMatters: Understanding the operational distinctions between Metrics (near-instant alerting, short-term data) and Logs (deep analysis, joins, and long-term retention) is essential for designing high-performance cloud monitoring solutions and scoring high on telemetry questions.
coreKnowledgePatterns: Data stores: Metrics are saved in a time-series database; Logs are saved in a Log Analytics workspace [184].
KQL Capability: Kusto Query Language supports advanced query types, including complex joins, filters, unions, and chart rendering [184, 192].

VM Agent requirement: VM host metrics are collected automatically. To ingest guest OS performance counters or syslog logs, a Log Analytics agent or Azure Monitor agent must be installed on the virtual machine [192].
GET exception: GET requests (read-only) are excluded from the Activity Log, which only logs PUT, POST, and DELETE calls [185].
examTraps: Assuming guest OS file or memory percentage metrics can be gathered without installing an agent on the virtual machine.
Using metric-based alert rules to trace administrative changes instead of Activity Log alerts.

awsComparison.keyDifferences: Azure Monitor unified both time-series metrics and log management under a single platform, while AWS historically separated CloudWatch (metrics) and CloudWatch Logs (log storage). To query logs in Azure Log Analytics, KQL is used [184]; in AWS, CloudWatch Logs Insights or Amazon Athena is required. Host metrics in both clouds are agentless, but OS-level metrics require the Azure Monitor Agent or AWS CloudWatch Agent.

highYieldNotes.topicName: Auditing and Compliance via Activity Logs
highYieldNotes.whyItMatters: The Activity Log is the primary mechanism to solve compliance requirements such as 'track who modified a resource and when.' It is heavily tested in scenarios requesting auditing configuration.
coreKnowledgePatterns: Administrative focus: It only tracks operations occurring at the subscription level, such as deploying VMs, resizing instances, or changing policy definitions [185].
Filtering filters: Users can query the Activity Log based on resource, resource group, event categories (Administrative, Policy, Service Health), operation name, or initiator (email) [185, 186].
Event limitations: Active logs exclude GET requests [185]. Resizing a virtual machine will generate a PUT/POST write event in the Activity Log.
Alerting: You can create alerts directly from Activity Log events to trigger notifications when specific configuration modifications occur [185].
examTraps: Believing that an Activity Log records file creation inside a VM's operating system or tracks read-only operations.
Choosing Diagnostic Settings to capture subscription-level audit logs when Activity Logs are already available globally by default.

awsComparison.keyDifferences: Both capture API level requests (who did what, when) within the cloud environment. However, Azure Activity Log is enabled by default with a rolling 90-day retention period, tracking administrative events without initial setup [185]. In contrast, AWS CloudTrail provides 90 days of management events free but requires configuring a 'Trail' to save logs to S3 for permanent storage. Azure Activity Log separates read (GET) from write (PUT/POST/DELETE) events [185], which parallels AWS's distinction between read-only and write-only management events.

highYieldNotes.topicName: Alerting Rules and Action Group Notifications
highYieldNotes.whyItMatters: Creating alert rules to trigger on CPU thresholds or guest OS disk space limits is a fundamental Azure administrator skill. Action Group sequence and composition is heavily queried in drag-and-drop questions.
coreKnowledgePatterns: Target Scope: An alert rule is target-scoped to a specific resource, resource group, or subscription [187].
Threshold options: Condition logic can evaluate metric-level statistics (Average, Minimum, Maximum) over a defined aggregation granularity and evaluation period [187].
Action Groups: These are reusable resources containing notification lists. Notifications include emailing specified subscription roles (e.g. Owner) or specific addresses (Email/SMS/Push/Voice) [188].
Automation blocks: Actions in an action group can trigger IT service management (ITSM) connectors, Webhooks, Logic Apps, Azure Functions, or Automation Runbooks to automate tasks [188, 192].
examTraps: Forgetting that to alert on custom guest metrics (e.g., volume disk space), the VMs must be configured to log performance data to a Log Analytics workspace before an alert rule can query it.
Assuming standard action groups can natively execute code without integrating with Azure Functions, Runbooks, or Logic Apps.

awsComparison.keyDifferences: Azure Monitor Alerts combine the alarm threshold rule and the notification routing into a unified workflow, though they refer to the notification resource as an Action Group [187, 188]. AWS uses CloudWatch Alarms to monitor metrics, which then publish to an Amazon SNS (Simple Notification Service) topic. Action Groups support direct native endpoints for automating remediations via Logic Apps, Runbooks, or Functions [188]; AWS requires subscribing an AWS Lambda function or Systems Manager Document directly to the SNS topic to achieve equivalent automated self-healing.

highYieldNotes.topicName: Network Watcher Diagnostics (IP Flow Verify & Next Hop)
highYieldNotes.whyItMatters: A massive focus of the AZ-104 exam. You must know exactly which tool is used for which specific scenario (NSG rule verification vs UDR route verification vs end-to-end latency diagnostics).
coreKnowledgePatterns: IP Flow Verify: Designed strictly to verify if NSG security rules block or allow traffic [189, 193]. It uses 5-tuple parameters (local IP/port, remote IP/port, protocol, and traffic direction) to show the rule name blocking/allowing traffic.

Next Hop: Scoped to diagnose routing issues by showing the route type (e.g. system route or Virtual Appliance / gateway) and route table used [189]. Highly useful when configuring User-Defined Routes (UDR) to virtual firewalls [189].

Connection Troubleshoot: Best for testing TCP or ICMP connection to any endpoint (VM, FQDN, IP) [190]. It returns latency details and hop-by-hop path information to identify exactly where a packet drops [190].
Effective Security Rules: Aggregates and displays all security rules associated with a VM's NIC and subnet to view overall rule priorities [193].
examTraps: Selecting Next Hop when a security rule (NSG) is blocking traffic, or choosing IP Flow Verify to troubleshoot a routing table/UDR issue.
Using ping directly inside the guest OS to troubleshoot security rules without verifying if ICMP is blocked by default in Azure NSGs.

awsComparison.awsEquivalent: AWS VPC Reachability Analyzer & Route Analyzer
awsComparison.keyDifferences: Azure Network Watcher bundles multiple diagnostic utilities (IP Flow Verify, Next Hop, Connection Troubleshoot) [193]. In AWS, VPC Reachability Analyzer performs a static configuration analysis of Security Groups, Network ACLs, Route Tables, and gateways to verify reachability. IP Flow Verify dynamically tests rule permissions based on a packet configuration [189, 193]. Next Hop matches AWS Route Analyzer's capability to trace routing tables. Unlike Azure's active probe-based Connection Troubleshoot [190], VPC Reachability Analyzer does not send actual data packets, performing only configuration-level path evaluation.

highYieldNotes.topicName: Network Watcher Flow Logs, Packet Capture, & Topology
highYieldNotes.whyItMatters: Managing high-level network monitoring. Exam questions frequently test regional restrictions for flow logs and the parameters required to deploy packet captures.
coreKnowledgePatterns: NSG Flow Logs regional restriction: Flow logs must write to a Storage Account located in the same geographic Azure region as the Network Security Group (NSG) [191, 193].

Packet Capture requirements: Network Watcher Agent extension must be installed on the target virtual machines to run packet capture. File saves can be bounded by max bytes, session bytes, or seconds [190].
Topology scope: Generated strictly at the Virtual Network (VNet) level [191]. It plots resources (VMs, subnets, route tables, NSGs, public IPs) and visualizes their topological connections [191].
Traffic Analytics: Processed by sending NSG Flow logs to a Log Analytics workspace [178]. This provides geographical map-based flow visualizations and traffic volumes.
examTraps: Selecting a storage account in a different region as the destination for NSG Flow Logs.
Assuming packet capture can run on virtual machines without installing the prerequisite Network Watcher Agent extension.

awsComparison.awsEquivalent: AWS VPC Flow Logs & VPC Traffic Mirroring
awsComparison.keyDifferences: Azure NSG Flow Logs record traffic per security group rule, while AWS VPC Flow Logs capture network interfaces (ENIs), subnets, or entire VPCs. Azure Flow Logs must store data in a storage account in the same region [191]. Azure Packet Capture runs directly on the VM (utilizing the Network Watcher extension) and writes to an S3-like Blob storage account [190]. AWS implements this at the hypervisor level via VPC Traffic Mirroring, forwarding raw ENI packets to a target elastic network interface or Network Load Balancer without requiring guest agents.

quizzes.questionText:
You have several virtual machines in a subscription. You need to identify which storage account to use for the flow logging of IP traffic from VM5. VM5 is connected to VNET4/Subnet1, which is in the East US region. VNET4 is associated with NSG1. You have the following storage accounts available:
- storage1 (general purpose v1, West US region)
- storage2 (general purpose v2, East US region)
- storage3 (BlobStorage, East US 2 region)
- storage4 (FileStorage, Central US region)

Which storage account should you identify?
quizzes.explanation: Network Watcher NSG Flow Logs must be stored in a standard storage account located in the same geographic Azure region as the Network Security Group (NSG) and virtual machines being monitored [191, 193]. Because VM5 and VNET4 are located in the East US region, the destination storage account must also reside in East US. Among the options, storage2 is the only storage account residing in the East US region (storage1 is in West US, storage3 is in East US 2, and storage4 is in Central US) [181]. Therefore, storage2 is the correct storage account to use.

quizzes.questionText: You plan to monitor virtual machine traffic across multiple virtual networks in the West US Azure region. You need to use Traffic Analytics in Azure Network Watcher to monitor virtual machine traffic. Which two resources should you create? Each correct answer presents part of the solution. NOTE: Each correct selection is worth one point.

options.text: a Data Collection Rule (DCR) in Azure Monitor

quizzes.explanation: To configure Traffic Analytics in Azure Network Watcher, you must first enable NSG Flow Logs [193]. Enabling NSG Flow Logs requires a standard Azure Storage Account as the target repository to write raw flow packets [191, 193]. Traffic Analytics then processes this raw packet flow data and aggregates it into a Log Analytics Workspace for visualization and querying [178]. Hence, a storage account and a Log Analytics workspace are the two prerequisite resources. Sentinel, Monitor Workbooks, and Data Collection Rules are not required to enable Network Watcher Traffic Analytics.

quizzes.questionText: You manage a virtual network named VNet1 that is hosted in the West US Azure region. VNet1 hosts two virtual machines named VM1 and VM2 that run Windows Server. You need to inspect all the network traffic from VM1 to VM2 for a period of three hours. Solution: From Azure Network Watcher, you create a packet capture. Does this meet the goal?
quizzes.explanation: Yes, creating a packet capture in Network Watcher meets the goal. Network Watcher packet capture is an on-demand session that allows you to capture inbound and outbound network packets on virtual machines [193]. You can specify duration constraints (e.g., three hours or 10,800 seconds), maximum packet size, and store the resulting file in an Azure Storage account or directly on the virtual machine's disk for subsequent inspection [190]. Therefore, packet capture is the correct tool.

quizzes.questionText:
You have an Azure subscription. You are configuring Network Watcher diagnostic tools to perform troubleshooting tasks. You need to select the correct diagnostic tool for each task:

Task 1: Identify whether an NSG security rule is preventing a virtual machine from communicating with another resource.
Task 2: Troubleshoot connectivity from a virtual machine to an external endpoint over a specific port, providing hop-by-hop latency metrics.

Which diagnostic tool should you select for each task?
quizzes.explanation: For Task 1, IP Flow Verify is the correct tool because it checks whether a security rule allows or denies inbound/outbound IP flow to/from a virtual machine, specifically identifying the exact NSG name and rule causing a drop [143, 193]. Next Hop is used to verify routing and UDRs rather than security group rules [189]. For Task 2, Connection Troubleshoot is correct because it actively tests TCP/ICMP end-to-end connectivity from a virtual machine to another VM, URI, FQDN, or custom IP port, and returns hop-by-hop diagnostic latency metrics to isolate where connectivity breaks down [190, 193].
